She was adding up her rectangles again, all thirty of them, and getting 8.8275, close to nine but not nine, and she understood for the first time that the difference wasn't an error. It was the distance to the limit. She wrote the two numbers down side by side and circled neither.

"How many would you need?" Danny asked. "Rectangles. To get to exactly nine."

"I don't know," Kate said. "Infinite, maybe. Try it." She slid the graph paper across the table and gave him the sharp pencil.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, attacked the Marxist social interpretation.
story:
Mr. Pavlik's classroom smelled like whiteboard marker and the radiator's particular burnt dust, and on the board he had written, in his handwriting that leaned like a man walking into wind, "Historiography: the history of history." Rachel copied it, then underlined it twice, which was what she did instead of understanding things.

The assignment sheet was one page. Trace how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800, it said, and cite at least six historians. Rachel had six names already, copied from the back of the textbook, and a thesis she'd drafted in the margin of her chemistry notes: for a long time everyone thought the Revolution was a class struggle, the bourgeoisie rising against the nobility, and then historians began to question that. It was a fine thesis except for one detail, which was that she could not name when the questioning started. The paragraph ended, at the moment, with the words "and then things changed," which even she knew was a sentence that meant nothing.

She brought the problem to Dana at lunch, because Dana had already written four pages and kept saying "per my outline" like a person who owned a filing cabinet. "You need the turning point," Dana said, spearing a tater tot. "The moment somebody first seriously went after the Marxist view. My brother says it was the sixties. Everything was the sixties, according to my brother."

"The whole decade?" Rachel said. "I can't cite a decade."

"Cite a person. Somebody in the sixties."

That night Rachel wrote the sentence anyway: In the 1960s, historians began to challenge the Marxist interpretation. It sat on her screen looking recalcitrant, refusing to become more specific, and she ate three crackers over the keyboard, which was against her own rules. She found names, dates attached to names, a confusing amount of both. One book called another book "influential." Another called the same book "overrated." She began to suspect that historians spent half their careers reviewing each other, like restaurants reviewing restaurants.

The confounder was the library's database, which sorted results by relevance in a way that seemed personal. She typed "French Revolution Marxist interpretation challenged" and got a lecture given in 1954, published in 1955 as a little pamphlet called The Myth of the French Revolution. She read the first page standing at the printer, because the chair by the computer was missing, someone had apparently needed it more than the library did. The lecture was by a man named Alfred Cobban, and it had been his inaugural lecture at University College London, which meant, she gathered, the speech you give when you've just gotten the job of professor, the one where you announce what you intend to do to your field. Cobban intended to do quite a lot. He went at the Marxist social interpretation the way her brother went at a durian, with visible delight and total commitment. Rachel thought of the verb "eviscerate," which Mr. Pavlik had used once about a student essay and which she'd had to look up, and thought that Cobban had done it to a half-century of scholarship in an hour.

So Dana's brother was wrong, ish. It wasn't the sixties. It was earlier, and it was one man, standing at a lectern in London in 1954, telling a room full of people that the story they all told was a myth.

The problem was the essay itself, which now had two options and Rachel had to choose. She could write the paper as a march: old view, Cobban, new view, done, tidy as a lab report. Or she could write what she'd actually seen in the database, which was that after Cobban, the Marxists didn't concede, they fortified, and the anti-Marxists fortified right back, and fifty years of argument produced not a winner but a field so divided that her textbook just... summarized both sides and moved on to Napoleon. She sat with this. The tidy version would get an A, probably. The other version was harder to outline and she couldn't yet see its shape.

She tried telling Dana about it the next day, in the hallway by the gym, where Dana was taping a poster for a French Club event that featured, inexplicably, a drawing of a baguette wearing a beret. "So it's not just that views changed," Rachel said. "It's that Cobban made them change by attacking, and the attack itself became the thing later historians had to respond to, so the field is like a family that had one huge fight at Thanksgiving in 1954 and everyone's still choosing sides."

"That's not an outline," Dana said.

"It's a thesis with a limp."

Dana considered the poster, smoothing a corner. "My brother's going to say it was still basically the sixties."

"He wasn't there. Nobody was there. That's the whole problem with historians."

Rachel wrote it that weekend anyway, the limping version, with Cobban's 1954 lecture as her hinge and both sides given their paragraphs, and an ending that admitted what she couldn't resolve: whether Cobban had found a flaw in the old view or only made it unfashionable, she couldn't say, and neither, as far as she could tell, could anyone else. On Monday she handed it in face-down, which changed nothing but felt safer. Mr. Pavlik took the stack, tapped it twice against the desk to align the pages, and read the first page of the top essay right there in front of them, unbothered, the way he did.

"Rachel," he said, without looking up, "do you know what happened to the chair by the library printer?"

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
The cones were still out from the morning session when Justine began her fourth consecutive day of sprints, though her legs had begun filing complaints somewhere around the second. She had planned the week herself, in a notebook with a cracked spine: Monday through Sunday, drills in the morning and conditioning at dusk, because the college tryouts were eleven days away and she intended to arrive at them faster than anyone on the field. On Thursday she timed herself at the forty-meter mark and found she was two tenths slower than Monday. On Friday she was slower still, and she stood at the touchline with her hands on her knees, watching her breath hang in the cold air, wondering what kind of arithmetic made you slower the harder you worked.

Her friend Priya sat on the bleachers with a granola bar and no plans to move. "You look like a phone at two percent," she said.

"I have eleven days."

"So does everyone, and everyone else is going home at six."

Justine wanted to adjudicate the matter right there, to weigh her plan against Priya's loafing and declare a winner, but the stopwatch had already voted, and it had not voted for her. She walked off the field carrying the notebook, and that night she did what she always did when something refused to make sense: she read. She read until a word surfaced in a coaching forum, a word she'd never heard spoken aloud, and she read the sentence under it three times. The body gets fitter during recovery, after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level. Not during the workout itself. She sat very still, because if that was true, then her whole week had been an argument against her own body, and she had been losing on purpose.

The next morning she found Priya stretching by the goalposts and read the word aloud from her phone. "Supercompensation," she said. "That's what they call it."

"Sounds like something a bank would do."

"Kind of is. You deposit the work, but the interest shows up later, when you're resting."

Priya chewed on that, and on the granola bar. "So your plan is what, to nap strategically?"

Justine laughed, but the question stayed with her through the warm-up laps, a gentle, nagging kind of wondering. How much rest? Enough to rebuild, not so much that everything you'd built quietly dissolved. The forum gave her shapes, not answers: a hard day, then an easy one; a hard week, then a lighter one. Nobody could tell her exactly where her own body fell on that curve, and she liked that and feared it in equal measure. She would have to test it on herself and watch what happened.

She rebuilt the week on a fresh page, leaving Sunday blank except for the word nothing, which she underlined twice. Monday became speed work after a full warm-up, the kind she used to skip as a formality, and Tuesday became passing and jogging, barely enough to sweat. Wednesday hard again. She taped the page inside her locker like a contract with a version of herself she hadn't met yet, and the odd thing was that the blank days frightened her more than the sprint days ever had. Rest felt like debt. Rest felt like the solvency of her training was in question, as if a single empty afternoon could bankrupt the whole enterprise.

On the first hard day of the new plan, she caught herself inventing reasons to add just one more session, and she made herself stop. On the rest day, she watched from the bleachers while the boys' team ran patterns, and she noticed things she never noticed while running: how the good players slowed down a half-second before receiving, how the keeper set her feet early. She was not, she realized, doing nothing. Her legs, meanwhile, did whatever quiet rebuilding they did, unobserved, unrehearsed.

Eight days in, she timed the forty again. Faster than Monday of the first week, faster than any day before. Not by much. Not by enough to guarantee anything about tryouts, which were now three days off, and she held that uncertainty carefully, turning it over like a stone. Maybe the rest had done it. Maybe the weather. Maybe she had simply measured badly before. She couldn't separate the threads, and she decided she could live with that, because the stopwatch had moved in the right direction and she had a theory with her name on it.

On the last morning before tryouts, she arrived before anyone else, laid out her cones, and began the warm-up she once would have skipped: jogging the width, then the strides, unhurried, deliberate. Priya came over the hill with her bag on one shoulder.

"You're here early."

"I'm testing something," Justine said, and set the stopwatch to zero.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
The robotics room smelled like solder and cold pizza, and the scrimmage was in four days. Thomas watched Yasmin run the arm code for the third time, and for the third time the gripper closed a half second late and knocked the block off the platform. Marcus, who had been with the team since freshman year and could read a motor stutter from across the room, said nothing. He wound a zip tie around a loose wire and told her the run looked smoother.

Afterward, in the hallway, Thomas asked him why. "Because she stayed until eleven last night," Marcus said. "You don't tell someone who stayed until eleven that her code is broken. You tell her it's getting better." Thomas said the code was getting worse, actually, and Marcus shrugged and said the scrimmage didn't really matter, which was a strange thing for someone who wanted the regional slot as badly as he did.

At home, Thomas's sister had left a book on the kitchen table next to her car keys. It was called Radical Candor, by Kim Scott, published in 2017, and he read forty pages standing up while the pasta water boiled. He did not expatiate on it to anyone that night; he kept it to himself, because he was not yet sure the idea survived contact with an actual person. The idea was simple enough on the page. Scott argued that good feedback combined caring personally about someone with challenging them directly, and that most people gave up one half to keep the other.

The next morning he tested the halves in his head like fractions. Marcus had the caring and had thrown out the challenge. There was also a version where you kept the challenge and lost the caring, and Thomas knew that version too, because he had done it in September, when he had told a sophomore her wiring diagram was a disaster and she had quit the team by Friday. He still thought about the diagram, which had been a disaster, and about Friday.

He found Yasmin in the library at lunch, sitting with her laptop open and the arm code on the screen. He had a prepared sentence, and he abandoned it. "The grip timing is off by about half a second," he said. "I saw it in all three runs yesterday. You stayed late, and I should have said something then instead of letting Marcus go on about smoother runs, because it isn't smoother, and you're the only one who can fix it." He heard how clumsy it sounded, the apology stacked on the criticism, but he let it sit there.

Yasmin did not look up right away. Then she turned the laptop toward him, and he saw that she already had the timing loop open, with a comment marked TODO beside a delay constant. "I found it at midnight," she said. "I was waiting to see if anyone else would." She closed the lid. "Marcus thinks being kind means never telling me I'm wrong. Do you know how loud that silence gets? It's like he thinks I'll shatter." Thomas said the book on the kitchen table called it radical candor, caring personally and challenging directly at the same time, and she said, "Somebody wrote a whole book about that? My mother runs a bakery on that."

They worked through the timing that period, and Yasmin was mercurial about it, cheerful when a fix worked, sharp and certain the world was against her for the ten minutes it didn't, so that Thomas had to adjust his tone three times before lunch ended. The fix turned out to be one constant, changed from 500 to 200, and the arm picked up the block on the first try after school. Marcus watched from the doorway with his arms crossed.

"You went behind my back," he said, though it had happened in an open library. Thomas said he hadn't, and then said that he had, a little, and that he was sorry for that part but not for the rest. Marcus said he wasn't paid enough for this, which was a joke, because none of them were paid, though the team's insurance carried some indemnity against injury at competitions, a fact Marcus recited whenever he wanted to sound like the adult in the room.

At the scrimmage, the arm ran clean through all three rounds, and they took the regional slot by four points. Afterward Marcus stood next to the field, unscrewing a battery cover that didn't need unscrewing. "Next time something's wrong with my code," he said, not quite looking at Thomas, "you'd tell me? Straight, like that." Thomas said he would, and honestly did not know if he would get the mixture right, whether caring and challenging could be held in the same hand every time, or only some of the time, and only by luck. "Okay," Marcus said, and handed him the screwdriver. "Hold this while I check the leads."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
Kyle signed the peer health form because Ms. Adeyemi had said the program needed boys, and because refusing would have meant explaining why he'd rather not, which he could not do. She called the position something like a trust, a fiduciary role, meaning that younger students would believe what he told them and he owed them accuracy instead of comfort. He wrote his name in the last box and then sat with the pen capped, staring at the curriculum sheet: consent, contraception, testing for infections. Three workshops, all of them his to run.

The first practice session went badly. He had the words, roughly, but they came out in the order of the handout, and when Dev from his chemistry class asked what "enthusiastic consent" actually meant at a party where everyone was drinking, Kyle said something about clear yeses that sounded like a poster. Dev said that was fine but didn't answer anything. Another boy started a tangential story about his cousin, and Kyle let it run because the silence after stopping it felt worse. Afterward he told Ms. Adeyemi he needed to see how any of this worked outside a classroom. She gave him a slip for the student clinic on Thursday.

He went partly for himself. He had decided this on the walk over, though the decision felt older than the walk. At the front desk a girl from his year, Priya, was already waiting with her hood up, and when she saw him she said, loudly enough for the receptionist to hear, that she was there for a friend. Kyle said nothing, because he understood the grammar of it, and sat two chairs away.

The nurse, whose badge said Rosa, called Priya first, then Kyle, and at some point the doors between the waiting room and the back stayed propped and the two of them ended up in the same consultation room, which Kyle suspected Rosa had arranged. Priya had come for a test and, having started talking, kept going: she'd been with a boy who hadn't used anything and hadn't asked, and she hadn't said to, and she kept circling the word "let," as if naming what she'd permitted would extenuate what he hadn't offered. Kyle said, carefully, that the asking was supposed to be his job too, not just her refusal. Priya looked at him like he'd spoken a language she'd read but never heard.

Rosa ran through the testing, the swab, the urine cup, the window periods, the clinic's quiet door on Delancey Street where nobody checked school ID. Then Priya asked about the pill versus other things, because a friend was on the pill and kept forgetting it, and Rosa pulled a plastic model from a drawer. She said hormonal IUDs and the implant fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once a clinician places them they don't depend on taking something daily. Kyle wrote it on his hand because his notebook was in his bag under Priya's coat, and Priya said, "Fewer than one in a hundred? For a whole year?" and Rosa nodded and moved on to cost and confidentiality.

Kyle ran his own numbers in the waiting room afterward, on the back of the curriculum sheet. The pill worked in theory, he knew, nearly always; it was the days, the ordinary days, that broke it. A method that survived forgetting was a different kind of method, not a better chemical but a different relationship to being human. He was not sure whether the workshop should say that or whether he was about to make a poster again.

The second workshop, he started differently. He asked who had ever forgotten something they meant to do every day, and thirty hands went up, including a teacher's at the back, and he wrote on the board what Rosa had said about IUDs and implants, the number, the year, the placement, the not depending on daily use, and let them copy it down. Then he asked them what the difference was between consent and not being stopped, and a quiet girl in the second row said, "One of them is a question that gets asked," and the room went still in a way that felt earned.

Dev raised his hand and asked whether asking felt strange, whether it killed things. Kyle said it could feel strange, and that he'd said it wrong once, too formally, and the other person had laughed, and they'd laughed, and then actually talked. He didn't say it always worked out. Some of what stayed uncertain he said out loud: that alcohol blurred things the way forgetting blurred the pill, and he didn't have a rule for exactly where the line was, only that being on the safe side of it cost less than the other side of it cost Priya, who was still waiting on results.

After the last session Priya found him by the water fountain. She said everything came back clear, and that she'd gone back and gotten the implant, and that she'd told the boy exactly what she hadn't said before, in sentences she'd rehearsed on the bus. Kyle asked if it had gone badly. She shrugged, and pulled the curriculum sheet out of her bag, the one he'd left in the clinic with his half-written numbers on the back, and smoothed it out and handed it to him.

"You can have this one back," she said. "I made my own."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: Leviticus 19:9-10 commands farmers not to reap the corners of their fields but to leave them, and the fallen gleanings, for the poor and the stranger.
story:
The festival had spread itself across the park in rows of tents, and Nathan had been assigned to the one with the long tables and photocopies, the one his rabbi called the Beit Midrash booth, though nobody at the festival knew what that meant. His actual assignment was simpler: sit there with a stack of texts and invite people to argue. He had agreed because Deborah had agreed, and Deborah, who was starting at Columbia in the fall and argued like other people breathed, had a way of making him feel both smaller and sharper at once.

The first hour was slow. A man asked whether they were selling dates. Then a woman from the Ethiopian food stall took a sheet, read it, and put it down without comment. When Deborah finally leaned over and said, "You have to actually talk to people," Nathan pushed a photocopy toward a teenager hovering nearby, a boy with a lanyard that read Youth Debate Institute, and asked, "Do you think a three-thousand-year-old farming law can tell anyone anything today?"

The boy, whose name was Marcus, sat down. The sheet held Leviticus 19:9-10, which commands farmers not to reap the corners of their fields but to leave them, and the fallen gleanings too, for the poor and the stranger. Marcus read it twice and said, "This is agricultural. Subsistence economy. It has nothing to say to me."

"Okay," Nathan said, "but why is it there at all? It's not ritual. It's not about the temple. It's sandwiched between laws about theft and lying." He was interpolating now, reading between the verses the way his grandfather had taught him, filling the gaps with reasoning rather than assertion, and he could feel Deborah watching to see whether he would do it honestly or just perform it.

"You could say that," Marcus said, "but that's a bromide. Ancient wisdom for modern life. Everyone says that about everything old. It doesn't mean the rule survives contact with, I don't know, gig work."

Nathan had prepared an answer, a good one, about how the law gives the poor a way to take food without begging, dignity built into the geometry of a field. But Deborah cut across him. "Read the last two words again," she said. "For the poor and the stranger. Not the poor of your own community. The stranger."

The moment felt smaller than seismic to everyone else, probably. To Nathan it rearranged something. He had spent the summer studying this passage with his grandfather, and he thought now of the note his grandfather had left inside his copy of the text before the surgery, a folded square of graph paper he had found only last week, tucked into the gutter of page 213. "You asked me last Passover whether the old rules still bind us," it read in his grandfather's cramped hand. "I gave you a rabbi's answer then. Here is a farmer's answer, from before I left the kibbutz: the field does not ask who is hungry. Only the farmer does. Decide which one you want to be. That is the whole question, and I am sorry to leave it with you."

He had carried the note to the festival without knowing why. Now he unfolded it on the table between Marcus and Deborah and let them read it, because he could not yet say aloud what it said, and because some arguments are better borrowed than spoken.

Marcus read it, then read the verses again, then said, "So your position is the law was never about farming."

"No," Nathan said slowly, working it out as he said it, which was either brave or careless. "My position is that the law is about the corner. The corner is the part you own but don't harvest. Whether your field is wheat or a paycheck or a Saturday, the question is whether there's a piece you leave on purpose, for someone you don't know. But I'm not sure about the gleanings part. The fallen stuff. The part you didn't plan to leave. I don't know whether the law means you have to let people take your accidents, and I don't know how you'd run a city on that."

Deborah opened her mouth, and for once closed it. Marcus was writing on the photocopy, underlining the stranger. "I came here for the dumplings," he said. "I'm going to be late for my own workshop."

"You could come back," Nathan said. "Tomorrow we're doing the one about not standing idly by."

Marcus stood, folded the photocopy into his pocket, and pointed at the graph-paper note still lying open on the table. "Frame that," he said. "Or at least don't lose it twice."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
story:
The book club met in the back room of the public library on the first Tuesday of the month, around a table with a coffee ring nobody ever wiped away. There were seven of them, and Ashton had been the youngest for two years, which he had decided not to mind. They were reading Wuthering Heights that month, and tonight Mrs. Okafor, the librarian who kept the club going out of what seemed like pure stubbornness, had asked them to look at one passage only: the scene where Catherine says she is marrying Edgar Linton even though her heart belongs to Heathcliff, because Heathcliff has been degraded by Hindley until he is beneath her.

Ashton had come prepared with two sets of notes on separate sheets, because his English teacher had taught them a Marxist lens and a feminist lens and he wanted to try both, the way you might try on two coats before buying either. The Marxist sheet said Catherine's choice was not romantic at all but economic; she was trading herself to the Lintons the way a family trades land in a bad harvest. The feminist sheet said Charlotte Bronte had to publish under a man's name, which meant every sentence in the book was written by someone pretending to be someone else, and that Catherine's options were a set of doors that all opened onto the same hallway. He read both sheets aloud, and then he stopped, because he realized he did not know which one to put down and which one to pick up.

"You're treating them like rivals," said Priya, who was seventeen and wanted, more than anything, to run the club someday, to choose the books and steer the discussion the way Mrs. Okafor did with her chin propped on her hand. "What if they're the same door?"

Ashton turned his pencil over. On the Marxist sheet he wrote in the margin, money decides who you may love. On the feminist sheet he wrote, and the money was never hers. That felt closer to true, though he wasn't sure it was finished.

Then Marcus, who was eighty-one and read with a magnifying card, asked the question that changed the evening. "Why are only two of the eleven books on our list this year written by women? Is that the canon or is that us?"

Nobody answered right away. Mrs. Okafor looked at the window, where the streetlight made a slow amber panel on the glass. Priya began flipping through her notebook, and Ashton, mostly to have something to do with his hands, got up and went into the stacks. He knew roughly where the criticism lived, and it was there, thin and green-jacketed, that he found A Room of One's Own, published in 1929. He had heard the title but never read it. He carried it back to the table, and Priya grabbed it before he sat down.

"Virginia Woolf says a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction," Priya read, and passed it on. "That's the whole argument in one line."

Ashton sat very still. His two sheets suddenly looked less like two coats and more like one coat with a lining. Woolf had put her finger exactly on the seam between his notes: if a writer needed money and privacy, then the shelf of classic novels was not a fair contest of talent but a record of who had been permitted to enter. The list wasn't a ranking; it was a ledger. The women who were missing had not failed to write. Some had been too poor, and some had written in a room that belonged to somebody else, and some, like Bronte, had worn a man's name just to get through the door. He said all this out loud, haltingly, and then he heard himself and said, "Although I can't prove the missing ones existed. That's the part that stays uncertain. Woolf's argument makes me expect them, but expectation isn't evidence."

"So the lens tells you where to look," Priya said, "not what you'll find." She had uncapped her pen and was writing on the club's planning sheet, which was technically Mrs. Okafor's job. "Motion for next year: half the list by women, half by men, and we decide the women first, while we're fresh."

Marcus seconded it before it was formally moved. Mrs. Okafor, instead of objecting, reached across the table and took the Woolf from Ashton's hand, and turned to the copyright page, and smiled at it in a way that suggested she had met it before, long ago, in a seminar she never talked about. "Carried it around for a whole winter once," she said. "Ask me someday." She wrote something small in the margin, in pencil, and slid the book back to Ashton, who saw, in her looping hand, the words his shelf is missing, and beside them a number: 1929. He put the book in his backpack, one of his two note sheets tucked inside it like a bookmark, and helped stack the chairs while Priya read her motion aloud a second time, for the record, and Marcus tapped his magnifying card on the table like a gavel.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Delayed-onset muscle soreness usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it.
story:
Tyson folded the towel into quarters and set it on the bleacher like a paper he was about to hand in, because what he'd brought to the court this morning was, in a way, homework. He had a spiral notebook with seven boxes drawn across the top of the page, one for each day, and inside each box he had written something: ball handling, sprints, legs, rest, shooting, rest, scrimmage. He was eighteen, a senior, and next fall he would be a walk-on at a college three states away, and the assistant coach there had emailed him a single line before summer break. Come in with a plan, not just a body.

The plan was the problem. Tyson had never planned anything athletic before; he had only played, the way water only flows downhill. When he felt good, he played more. When he felt wrecked, he stopped. Now he sat on the bleachers at the far end of Emerson Park waiting for Rique, who was late in the way Rique was always late, and he studied his seven boxes and wondered whether rest days were for people who lacked hunger or for people who understood it.

Rique arrived with his history textbook under one arm, because summer session existed and Rique's mother did not believe in an idle July. "I got a test Monday," he said, dropping the book on the concrete. "On Iran. Whole thing's basically who turned a monarchy into a theocracy and who got left out." He bent to tie his shoe. "You still doing that coach's thing?"

"Trying." Tyson turned the notebook toward him. "First week I did everything hard, every day. Figured I'd rest when I was dead."

"And?"

Tyson laughed, short and rueful. "Monday I felt incredible. Tuesday I felt incredible. Wednesday morning I couldn't get down the stairs sideways." He mimed gripping a banister with both hands. "Thursday was worse. Then Friday it kind of let go of me."

Rique squinted at the notebook as if it were in a foreign alphabet. "So you got hurt?"

"No, that's the thing. Nothing was hurt. It was just soreness, the delayed kind, but it didn't show up right after the workout like I expected. It peaked days later." He tapped the page. "Somewhere between twenty-four and seventy-two hours after the first hard day. So I kept adding more on top of it because I felt fine, and then it all landed on me at once."

"Huh," Rique said, in the tone of a person filing something away for no reason he could name.

They played one-on-one to eleven, and Tyson lost 11-7, which was closer than usual, and his legs felt heavy in a way he recognized now as Tuesday's work arriving on Friday. Between games he sat on the ball and looked at his boxes again. The problem wasn't that he had trained too hard, exactly. It was that he had made one way of thinking fight another. The old Tyson said pain proved effort, and rest was a moral failure. The new Tyson was trying to believe that a rest day was a tool, like a screen or a crossover. He didn't fully believe it yet. He believed it maybe sixty percent, the way you believe a bridge you haven't driven across.

The two perspectives kept circling each other all week, and he let them argue in his head while his hands did the work. Monday: warm-up first, ten minutes, easy movement until his shoulders stopped feeling like borrowed equipment, then skills, moderate. He wrote the warm-up into the box and then, after some thought, into every box, because a warm-up wasn't an event, it was a door. Tuesday: nothing but stretching and the stationary bike, and he hated the stillness until he noticed that his shot was sharper on Wednesday than it had been in a month. Thursday: legs, hard, but he stopped one set earlier than the old Tyson would have, and he made himself write why in the margin. Feels fine now. That means nothing. Peaks later.

Saturday he drove to the court at seven because the heat came early and the court's blacktop by afternoon could desensitize the soles of your feet until you couldn't feel a pebble under your pivot foot, and he liked to know what was under him. Rique was already there, sitting on the bleachers with his textbook open to a chapter called "1979."

"You know what's funny," Rique said, not looking up. "The way they talk about a revolution, it's all one event, one date. But it was years. The real change came months after anybody was looking." He shut the book. "That's on the test, probably."

Tyson stood at the free-throw line and bounced the ball three times, his small ritual, and thought that his legs had arrived somewhere new without his noticing, the way things that matter apparently do. The notebook sat open on the bleacher with Sunday's box still empty except for the word he'd written and rewritten: rest, rest, rest. He wasn't sure the plan would survive contact with a real college weight room, or that sixty percent belief would hold. But he shot the ball, and it went in clean, and from somewhere behind him Rique called, "Again," so he did it again.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: False friends are words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning; Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed.
story:
The debate topic was printed on the whiteboard in Señora Ives's handwriting: should schools monitor students' social media for signs of distress? Five minutes, entirely in Spanish, no notes after the first thirty seconds. Chloe had volunteered because Marcus had dared her to, which was a bad reason, and because she actually had an opinion, which was a worse one, since opinions in a second language had a way of dissolving mid-sentence.

She practiced in the empty drama room at lunch, arguing with the folding chairs. Her position was the complicated one: monitoring might catch some kids, but it also taught everyone else to hide better, and a system that only worked when people were careless seemed to her tautological, proving only what it assumed. She did not know the Spanish for tautological, so she said it in English and kept going, and the chairs offered no objection.

Her opponent was Dani, who had lived in Madrid until fifth grade and spoke the way water runs, without visible effort. Dani's side was the simple one: kids were struggling, adults should pay attention. Chloe suspected it was also partly a truism dressed as an argument, the kind of sentence nobody could disagree with and nobody could use, but she needed Spanish words to say so, and she had exactly four days to find them.

On Wednesday she found "patologizar" in the dictionary app, hovering near the English word she wanted, pathologize. She wrote it on her palm in pen. Monitoring students' posts, she would argue, tended to pathologize ordinary teenage misery, the sad song posted at midnight that meant nothing, the joke that meant even less. Whether that was worth the risk of missing the kid who meant everything, she still had not decided. That was the part that kept her awake.

The debate happened Friday, fourth period, with the whole class pulled into a circle of desks and Señora Ives scoring on a clipboard. Dani went first and was flawless for two minutes, and then Chloe stood, and her mouth went dry in the specific way it does when you have memorized the wrong thing perfectly. She got through her opening. She gestured at the word on her palm without looking at it, and it came out, patologizar, and Dani nodded slowly, conceding the ground.

Then Chloe reached for the sentence she had rehearsed most, the one about how the program would humiliate students, and she said embarazada instead of avergonzada, because the two words had shadowed each other in her head all week. A ripple of laughter went around the circle. Sam actually fell off the arm of his chair. "Embarazada means pregnant," Dani said, grinning, "not embarrassed. False friends. They look alike, they aren't."

Chloe's ears burned. She looked at the clock: two minutes and forty seconds left, an ocean. She could quit, or she could stand there bleeding out in front of thirty people. Instead she took the word and kept it. "De acuerdo," she said slowly, "estoy embarazada de errores," and she did not fully know if that worked grammatically, but the laughter turned with her, warm now instead of at her. She argued the rest in plain, short sentences, simpler than she had planned, and slower. When she could not find a word she circled it, the way you point at a shape you cannot name. Señora Ives wrote something long on the clipboard.

Afterward, in the hallway, Dani caught up with her. "You know you lost, right? On points. Your grammar fell apart after the laughing." Chloe said she knew. "But it was the better argument," Dani went on, as if this were a technical complaint. "The part about how monitoring teaches hiding. I hadn't thought of that. My dad's a counselor and I still hadn't." She stopped at the water fountain. "Also, nobody ever survives saying embarazada wrong. Usually they stop talking. You sped up."

Chloe told her about the dictionary app, the palm, the four days of lunch in the drama room. Dani drank, wiped her mouth, and pulled out her phone. "I made a list once. False friends, like forty of them. My cousin sent it. Wanna see?" She scrolled, and Chloe leaned in, and there in the glow between them was the whole minefield, laid out in two neat columns.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: In most jurisdictions traffic already on a highway has the right of way, so a merging driver must adjust speed to fit a gap rather than expect others to make room.
story:
The kitchen smelled of burnt toast and road dust, because Aaron had been sitting at the counter for twenty minutes reading the driver's manual while his mother scraped the black off the bread with the edge of a knife. He had his test in four days. He could do three-point turns in his sleep, could reverse around corners, but parallel parking still undid him, and merging onto the highway undid him more. His father had taken him out that morning for practice, and it had gone badly in a way Aaron was still turning over.

"You're quiet," his mother said, setting a plate in front of him.

"The truck didn't move."

"What truck?"

"On the ramp. I got on the acceleration lane and there was a truck in the right lane and I kept waiting for it to move over, and Dad grabbed the wheel and we ended up on the shoulder." He pushed the toast around the plate. "Dad said the truck should have gone over. He was honking at it after, out the window, on the shoulder, like that helped."

His mother sat down across from him with her own coffee. "And what did you think?"

Aaron had thought the truck driver was rude. He had also thought, in a smaller voice he didn't like, that he had been the one going sixty down a ramp expecting a gap to open. "I don't know. Everyone always says let people in. Be courteous. Mom, in school they make a whole thing of it, hold the door, make room."

"That's a door," his mother said. "That's one person and one doorway."

He turned the manual around so she could see the page, though he knew she wasn't going to read it. He had found the line last night and read it four times. "In most jurisdictions traffic already on the highway has the right of way," he said. "So the merging driver adjusts speed to fit a gap instead of expecting others to make room." It had struck him as almost metaphysics, this idea that the road had an order no one had invented, that courtesy was a separate thing from law, that you could be generous and still be wrong. His father's honking had been a kind of philosophy too, just a louder one.

"So practice the gap," his mother said. "You can do that tonight with your father, if he's stopped being furious at trucks."

"He's not furious. He just thinks everyone should make room. He drove delivery for nine years, he thinks the road is a place where people look out for each other."

"And you think?"

The kitchen tap dripped, one slow drop, then another. Aaron looked at the window over the sink, at the gravel of the driveway, which was friable stuff, pale and crumbling at the edges where the rain got at it, and he thought about how his father's way of driving assumed a soft world and the manual assumed a hard one, and how neither of them was exactly wrong. He had spent the whole summer being told to put himself forward, apply early, email the professor, introduce yourself at orientation, make yourself a gap. He had also been told, by the same people sometimes, to read the room, to wait, to fit in. He had never once been told how to tell those two instructions apart.

"I think both things," he said. "You make room for people when you can, and you don't count on it. You look for the gap and you take the gap that's actually there, not the one that should be there." He heard how it sounded, like a kid trying on a suit. "I don't know how you do both at the same time, though. Dad drives like the gap will appear. Maybe it usually does, for him. Maybe that's the problem, it usually does."

That evening they went out again, his father quieter now, hands loose on his knees. On the ramp to Route 9 there was a line of cars and no truck, but there was a blue sedan holding its lane, and Aaron, instead of drifting toward it with his blinker pleading, eased off the gas, let the sedan pass, found the gap behind it, and slid in at matching speed. His father said nothing for a full mile, then said, "Better."

They parked on Elm Street under the big maples, between a mailbox and a Buick, and Aaron backed in on the second try, close to the curb, crooked by a hand's width but inside the lines. His father got out and walked around the car once, kicking the tire, then leaned in the open window.

"Tomorrow," he said, "do it again without the mailbox to aim at."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Electric field strength can be measured in volts per metre or in newtons per coulomb, and the two units are equivalent.
story:
The skate park emptied toward dusk, the way a tide leaves things behind: one boy still grinding the low rail, a cluster of younger kids trading a board back and forth, and Anais on the flat concrete apron with her review book open on her knees. She had chosen the spot deliberately, or told herself she had, because the apartment was too quiet and the library closed at six. Really she liked the noise. The clatter of wheels on coping made a rhythm she could think against.

Her pencil hovered over the problem. Two parallel charged plates, a point between them, and the question of the field strength at that point. She had drawn the plates as two clean lines, shaded the space between, and marked the point with a small x, and then she had stopped, because the answer she got and the answer in the back of her mind refused to agree.

"Move your foot," said a voice. A board shot past her ankle, and its rider, a saturnine girl in a grey hoodie, wheeled back around and stopped. "You're in the landing zone."

Anais gathered her things six inches to the left. The girl watched her shuffle the papers, then looked closer at the drawing. "Is that physics?"

"Take-home test review. Not the actual test." Anais covered the page partly out of habit, then uncovered it. "I keep getting the same number as my friend Tomas, but he says I did it wrong."

The girl rolled the board back and forth under her feet, an idle metronome. Her name, it turned out, was Rafa, and she was repeating twelfth grade at the school across town, and she sat down on the concrete as if it were furniture. "Show me."

Anais walked her through it, or tried to. The plates, the point between them, the value she had computed. "Tomas got the same number, but he wrote his answer in different units, and he says mine is wrong because of that. We argued about it for twenty minutes on Thursday. He got this face, like, the exact face of a person who knows he's right."

"And you got the same number." Rafa picked up the pencil and turned it over. "Both times. The exact same number."

"That's the part I can't stop thinking about." Anais pulled both versions from her folder: hers with one set of units, Tomas's with the other. She laid them side by side on the concrete, delimited by a crack in the slab as if the ground itself were drawing the boundary between them. "How can the same number with different units both be the answer? One of them has to be wrong. Unless." She stopped.

Rafa was grinning, a slow unguarded grin that broke the hooded, saturnine set of her face. "Unless they're the same thing."

"Volts per metre and newtons per coulomb," Anais said, mostly to hear the words outside her head. "They're equivalent." She said it twice more, quieter. It felt less like learning a new fact than like discovering that two rooms she had been living in shared a wall, that someone had cut a door and she had simply never turned the right handle. All afternoon she had assumed one of them was an artifice, a trick of notation Tomas had invented to win the argument, and instead both were real, both were true, and neither had to defeat the other.

She tried to figure out which one she preferred, and found she could not decide. Volts per metre described the field one way, newtons per coulomb another, and the fact that they met at the same value made the whole thing feel larger, not smaller. She wondered whether other disagreements were like this, whether half the arguments she had ever witnessed were two people standing in the same room describing different walls. She could not prove that, and she was honest enough with herself to admit it: the equivalence was certain, and everything she was spinning out from it was only a guess she liked.

"Your friend's going to be unbearable," Rafa said, standing, sliding her foot onto the board.

"He's going to say I only texted him because I wanted to concede." Anais was already typing the message, thumb hovering. Behind her the boy on the rail landed something clean and loud, and the younger kids whooped, and the floodlights buzzed on all at once, turning the bowls pale blue.

"Tell him you were both right," Rafa said, and pushed off toward the far ramp.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including those who already have hypertension.
story:
Hunter had promised the pharmacy manager he would come in on Saturdays to shadow the counter clerks, mostly to see whether he could stand a year of it before applying to the health sciences program. He had not expected his mother to be waiting in the lobby when he arrived that morning, holding a slip of paper like it was a parking ticket.

"The dentist took it," she said. "Before the cleaning. One thirty-eight over eighty-eight. The hygienist said to have it checked again somewhere."

She had gone in for a chipped filling and come out with a number attached to her, and she kept looking at the slip as if it might change if she read it enough times. Hunter asked whether the dentist had said anything else, and she said he'd told her to follow up with her regular doctor, and then he'd gone back to his drill.

At the pharmacy there was a machine near the blood pressure aisle, a chair with a cuff built into the armrest. Hunter asked one of the clerks, a second-year nursing student named Priya, whether he could practice with it, and she said sure, on his own arm first, so he would know what a normal reading felt like. The cuff squeezed tight and then let go, and the number came up small and unremarkable. Then his mother sat down, and the machine worked its slow mechanical grip, and the screen said one thirty-six over eighty-six.

Priya glanced over from the register. "Twice that high in one morning means something," she said. "That's what the doctor will call hypertension when he confirms it. You should write both numbers down for the appointment."

Hunter wrote them on the back of the dentist slip. His mother said she wasn't going to beseech anyone over a number, she was going to make an appointment like a normal person, but she said it lightly, and she let him hold the slip afterward.

He spent the rest of the morning shelving antacids and reading the pamphlet rack while the counter was quiet. One pamphlet, printed by some heart association, had a page on blood pressure and what changes it. He read that regular aerobic exercise, the kind that gets you breathing harder, like brisk walking or cycling, done on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, and that this held true even for people who already had hypertension. He read the page twice, then turned it over looking for the catch, for a paragraph of restrictions, and found only a note about starting slowly if you'd been inactive, which his mother certainly had been since winter.

The trouble was the word aerobic. His father had bought a stationary bike years ago and hung shirts on it, and his mother walked only at the grocery store. But the pamphlet had not said intervals or a gym membership; it had said brisk walking, most days, and Hunter thought about the loop past the middle school and down along the greenbelt, where the trail followed the creek above the buried aquifer that supplied half the town's water. Three miles, flat, lit until nine. He did the math on a receipt: thirty-five minutes out, thirty-five back, five evenings a week, most days with a spare for rain.

When his mother came back for her car keys at lunch, he laid the pamphlet on the counter beside the slip with the two readings. "The dentist gave you a free toothbrush," he said. "That part was free and fine. The number is the part that isn't a gift, it's just information." She said the toothbrush had felt slightly gratuitous, coming as it did with a bill, and he laughed, and then he tapped the page. "This says walking works. Brisk walking, or cycling, most days of the week. It lowers blood pressure in a lot of people. Even people who already have the high kind. Even people like you, probably."

"Probably," she repeated.

"That's what it says. Many people. Not all people. I'm not pretending it's a promise." He had thought about this while shelving, about the difference between the pamphlet's careful many and the certainty he wanted to hand her, and he decided the honest version was better than a flattering one. "You still see the doctor. But in the meantime, there's this."

She looked at the loop he'd drawn on the receipt, past the school, along the creek. "Thirty-five minutes," she said. "I'd want to complain the whole first mile."

"Complain quietly. That can be aerobic too."

They started that evening, the two of them, after the heat broke. She talked for the first half mile about the dentist's bill and about a cousin who had taken up running and become insufferable, and Hunter said nothing, only kept the pace brisk, his arms swinging, his breath deepening the way the pamphlet implied it should. Near the creek the air smelled of wet gravel and cut grass. At the turn-around point she stopped, hands on her hips, breathing hard, and looked back up the trail toward the school lights.

"Same time tomorrow?" she said.

"Most days," Hunter said. "That's the part that matters."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: A zero derivative does not guarantee a maximum or minimum: f(x) = x cubed has derivative zero at x = 0, but its graph keeps rising through that point.
story:
The corner store on Delmore Street had a stool behind the register that Makayla had claimed as her study carrel since October, and Mr. Okafor had stopped objecting around November. She spread her calculus worksheet on the counter between the lottery tickets and a jar of friable-looking peanut brittle that had been there since before her midterm. The problem asked her to find the maximum of some cubic, and she was fairly sure she had it in three lines.

"You buying anything tonight?" Mr. Okafor asked. He was on the phone again with the vending machine company, arguing about a clause in his contract, something about indemnity, the word arriving like a stone dropped into his side of the conversation. He wanted them to pay for the machine that had shocked a customer, or at least to admit the machine existed. "Then why is it in my store," he said, and listened, and rolled his eyes at Makayla as though she were a co-conspirator.

She took the derivative the way the textbook had shown her, brought the exponent down, subtracted one, and set the whole thing equal to zero. x equals zero. She circled it and wrote maximum in confident block letters, the way you sign a receipt for something you haven't inspected. "Done," she announced, mostly to feel the word in the air.

Her cousin Deja came in for the Arizona teas she bought every evening before her shift at the nursing home, dropped two dollars thirty in nickels on the counter, and leaned over the worksheet with the proprietary interest of someone who had failed precalculus twice. "That says maximum?"

"Derivative's zero there," Makayla said. "That's the rule. Where it flattens out is the top of the hill."

Deja squinted. She had a way of looking at numbers as though they had personally insulted a relative. "You drew the hill yet?"

"I don't need the hill. The algebra is the hill."

Mr. Okafor hung up the phone with the slow deliberateness of a man who had not won. "When I bought this store," he said, unasked, "the previous owner told me the slushie machine was the best thing in it. Best thing. It leaked from the first week." He said the previous owner's name the way other people vilify a dictator, with feeling and a long history. "On paper it was perfect. Papers flatten things."

Makayla was about to say that math wasn't the same as a slushie machine when Deja plucked the pen from her hand and drew axes across the whole worksheet, rude and unapologetic. "So what's the actual function?" Makayla read it off the page, and Deja, who could plot points slowly but stubbornly, marked the curve through them. It came up from the lower left, rose, rose further. At x equals zero there was a kind of hesitation, a breath, and then it kept climbing to the upper right, patient as a staircase.

"Your hill," Deja said, tapping the point with the cap, "is a hallway."

Makayla looked at it for a long moment, at the little flat spot where the derivative went to zero and the graph went right on rising through it as if nothing had been decided there. Her three confident lines sat above the drawing like testimony that had just been contradicted. She crossed out maximum. She did not write anything in its place, because she wasn't yet sure what was true there, only what wasn't. "So zero just means it flattens," she said slowly. "It doesn't promise you a top. You have to look." It occurred to her that every answer she'd circled this semester deserved the same suspicion, and that this was either exhausting or the whole point.

Mr. Okafor rang up the teas and slid a napkin toward her, on which he had written, in pharmacist's handwriting, the word indemnity underlined twice. "You are going to be a lawyer," he said. "Tell me what this means so I know whether to be angry."

She picked up the pen again and started graphing the next problem before answering anything, all the way to its edges.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, one Frida wears a white European-style Victorian dress and the other wears a traditional Tehuana dress, a contrast often read as her mixed European and Mexican heritage.
story:
Madeline would tell anyone who asked that she had never cared much about art, which was true except for the summer she was fifteen and spent three days copying postcards of paintings at the kitchen table, an episode she preferred to forget. It was her mother who had signed her up for the Saturday critique workshop at the community art studio, and it was Madeline herself who had failed to say no, which she later insisted amounted to the same thing. The studio smelled of turpentine and old coffee, and the far wall was covered in student watercolors pinned up like evidence.

The instructor, a wiry man named Denny who mostly refereed rather than taught, taped a print of The Two Fridas above the drying rack and told them to talk. Madeline sat between Priya and Carlos, who had already begun their argument before the tape was smoothed flat.

"The European one is the real one," Priya said. "Look at how she's painted, the one in the white Victorian dress. She's holding the scissors. That's the one doing the cutting, so that's the one in control."

Carlos shook his head. "The Tehuana dress. The traditional one. That's who she actually was, that's the Mexican side, that's her. The white one is a costume."

"A costume," Priya repeated, in the tone of someone filing the word away as evidence against him.

Madeline had been looking at the print the way Denny had taught them the week before, not at what the painting meant but at how it was built. Two women seated on a bench, hands joined at the center, exposed hearts connected by a thin artery that ran from one to the other. The left figure in white, the right in the Tehuana dress, holding a small portrait in place of the artery's end. She had written in her notebook: symmetry, but broken symmetry. The sky behind them was storm-colored, and the little clouds at the horizon seemed to presage something, though she couldn't say what.

"You're both doing the same thing," she said, and immediately wished she hadn't, because both of them turned.

"What thing," Carlos said.

"Cutting her in half. Picking one side and calling it the real one." She pointed at the print. "Look at the artery. It runs from the European Frida's cut heart to the Tehuana Frida's intact one. She painted them joined. That's the composition, that's the whole structure of it."

Priya leaned in. "So which one is real?"

Madeline had an answer ready, or believed she did, and this is where her account of the afternoon begins to disagree with itself. She said, later, that she had answered confidently, but at the time she remembered pausing long enough for the radiator to click twice. "Both," she said finally. "Her father was European and her mother was Mexican, and the two dresses are the two sides of that, and the painting won't let you choose, which is the point. The hands are clasped. She's holding her own hand."

Carlos sat back. "So the self-portrait is of two selves."

"Or of one self that won't split, and the blood just goes back and forth." She was aware that she was now saying something she hadn't thought until she said it, that the sentence had built itself out of the paint rather than out of her, and she distrusted the feeling, which was close to vanity.

Denny wandered over with his coffee. "Color?" he said, which was his way of asking a question without asking it.

"White against the reds and the dark blues," Madeline said. "The white dress is this kind of impermeable surface, nothing gets in, blood goes everywhere else but the dress stays white. And the Tehuana dress has the warm colors, it belongs to the picture's body. I don't know if that makes one of them more real. Maybe it makes the white one the more painted one. Maybe those aren't the same thing."

She was thinking, though she did not say so, of the postcards at the kitchen table three years ago, of a girl who had copied a Kahlo without knowing anything about her and had liked only the bright dress. It occurred to her that she had been on Carlos's side all along without knowing there was a side to be on, that her whole original liking had been a kind of complicity with an argument she'd never heard. She wasn't sure that was honest. Maybe she just liked the colors.

"Fine," Priya said, uncapping a marker to write on the chart paper. "Both are real, they're connected, the two dresses are the two heritages, European and Mexican, happy? That's your considered position?"

"That's my position today," Madeline said. "The symbolism part I'm sure about. Whether she liked either of them, whether one of them was a mask, that I can't get from the paint. I can't get her from the paint. I can only get what she put there."

The radiator clicked again. Carlos pulled the print down off the wall without asking Denny and laid it flat on the table between them, so close that the two joined hands were directly under the lamp.

"Show me where you said the artery starts," he said.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Readers usually detect an unreliable narrator through contradictions, such as other characters' words or the events themselves not matching what the narrator claims.
story:
Nevaeh spread the novel across her grandmother's kitchen table, next to a bowl of figs and a pad of yellow sticky notes she'd found in the junk drawer. The assignment was due Monday, her first for the college course she'd been allowed to start early, and the prompt asked one question: how does the narrator's point of view shape the reader's trust? She had read the book twice and still couldn't tell whether she believed a word the man said.

"Your grandfather used to annotate books like that," her grandmother said, setting down two glasses of iced tea. "Colored tabs everywhere. Looked like the book had been attacked by a small festive animal."

"He used tabs?"

"He used whatever was near him. Once, bookmarks made of bacon." Her grandmother sat and peeled a fig with more dignity than the bacon story deserved. "So what's the trouble?"

"The trouble is the narrator keeps saying he's the only honest man in the book, and I keep believing him, and then something happens that makes me feel like a fool for believing him."

"Have you tried catching him at it?"

Nevaeh paused with a sticky note half-peeled from the pad. "Catching him?"

"Readers usually detect an unreliable narrator through contradictions, like other characters' words or the events themselves not matching what the narrator claims," her grandmother said, tapping the table. "That's what your grandfather used to say, anyway. He said it in that elocution of his, like he was announcing a verdict in court."

Nevaeh pulled the novel toward her and began to work. Whenever another character said something that clashed with the narrator's account, she slapped a yellow note on the page. Whenever the events themselves went against him, a scene he described as tender that left someone crying, a room he called empty that the text plainly showed was full, she used a blue note. It was slow going and strangely exhilarating, like fishing where the fish keep striking, and by late afternoon the book bristled with paper like a hedgehog dressed for a party.

"You've missed dinner," her grandmother said from the doorway, but she said it softly, watching.

"Look at this." Nevaeh fanned the pages so the notes fluttered. "Every yellow note, someone contradicting him, is in the first half. Every blue one, the events turning on him, is in the second half. That's a pattern. It's like the author trained me to trust him before breaking me in half." She frowned at her own words. "Although maybe the pattern is mine, not the book's. Maybe I just got better at noticing things as I went."

"That," said her grandmother, "is the most intelligent thing you've said all day, and you've said several intelligent things, including asking where the sticky notes were."

Nevaeh remembered, then, the summer she was nine, sitting on this same porch with her grandfather while he read her a chapter of a pirate book, doing all the voices. When the pirate captain swore he'd never abandoned a crew, the parrot in the story kept squawking "Gave 'em up! Gave 'em up!" and nine-year-old Nevaeh had shouted that the parrot was lying, because the captain seemed so sad and honest. Her grandfather had laughed until he had to set the book down. "The parrot," he'd finally managed, "does not have a horse in this race, sweetheart." She had not understood him then. She understood him now, the way the smallest witness with nothing to gain could knock down the grandest self-defense, and she wished she could tell him so, and she suspected he knew anyway.

She tested the pattern against it. The parrot had contradicted the captain early, which broke her neat yellow-then-blue theory, but then, the pirate book was a comedy, and hers was not, and maybe trust worked differently when a book was joking. She wrote that down too, in the margin, in handwriting that could only be called inchoate, the letters crowding each other like passengers on a late bus.

At the kitchen table she drafted the essay until midnight, and her grandmother drifted past occasionally in her robe to refill the tea without being asked. The thesis, when it finally surfaced, was not clean: the narrator was unreliable, she argued, and the book built trust before withdrawing it, and the evidence had a pattern she could show, though she admitted she could not be certain the pattern wasn't partly her own attention ripening. She let the uncertainty stay in the paragraph. It felt more honest than a tidy ending, and anyway the deadline was not interested in her soul.

Her grandmother read the last page over her shoulder, one hand resting on the back of Nevaeh's chair. "He'd have put a bacon bookmark in that," she said.

"He'd have said the parrot was the hero."

"He did say that. Twice. Now close the book before you dream in sticky notes."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a presidential system, the president is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term and cannot be removed simply because the legislature disagrees with them.
story:
The line outside the community centre had begun to form before six, when the sky over the car park was still the grey of an unwashed window, and Charlie stationed herself near the door with a clipboard she was not entirely sure she needed. Her job was simple: greet voters, direct them to the correct table, and keep the queue moving. She was sixteen, three years too young to vote, and had taken the volunteer shift anyway because her mother had said that watching democracy was the next best thing to practising it, and because Charlie wanted, with a fierceness she did not fully understand, to know what she would be walking into when her turn finally came.

Priya arrived at half past seven, slipping through the doors with a canvas bag of pastries for the volunteers, though she lingered by Charlie's table instead of leaving. Priya's family had moved here three autumns ago, and she still spoke about politics the way other people spoke about weather, as something that changed your plans whether you liked it or not. "Back home," she said, peeling the foil off a pastry, "we're having an election too. The prime minister called it early. She has to, if she loses the confidence of parliament." Charlie filed that phrase away, confidence of parliament, the way she filed formulas before a test, without yet knowing where it fit.

Marcos came at nine with his grandmother, a small woman in a green coat who voted first and then waited on a folding chair by the noticeboard, reading every poster twice. Marcos had lived here for two years and still kept a photograph of the presidential palace in his pencil case, which Charlie knew because he had shown it to the whole class in September. He drifted over to Priya and Charlie during a lull, and somehow, in the way of conversations between people standing too long in one place, they began to argue about which system was better, parliamentary or presidential, each of them defending the country they knew.

"You can get rid of our leader in weeks," Priya said. "If parliament decides it doesn't have confidence in her, she's finished. A vote, and she's out." Marcos folded his arms. "That's chaos. Our president serves the full term. The whole country votes for the president directly, separately from the congress, on a fixed day, for a fixed number of years. You can't just kick her out because congress disagrees with her." He said it with the flat certainty of someone reciting gravity. Priya opened her mouth to object, then closed it, which for Priya was remarkable.

Charlie had been half listening, mesmerized by the rhythm of the queue, the shuffling feet, the soft clatter of the stamp at table two, and the argument pulled her back like a hand on her sleeve. "So wait," she said slowly, turning the clipboard over in her hands. "The difference isn't who votes. It's whether the leader's job depends on keeping the parliament happy." She looked from one to the other. "Priya's prime minister can be removed if parliament turns on her. Marcos's president can't be, not just for that. The president is elected separately, for a fixed term, and stays even when the legislature hates her." Marcos nodded; Priya, after a moment, nodded too.

"It means our elections are about everything at once," Priya said. "Party, leader, platform, all in one vote. Yours are two separate votes." "And ours means the president doesn't have to panic every time congress gets bellicose," Marcos said, glancing toward his grandmother, who had overheard the word and raised an eyebrow at him. Charlie laughed despite herself. The same fact seemed to open in two directions at once: one system made a leader accountable day by day, the other made her stable year by year, and she could not see how a country got to have both.

The presiding officer leaned out of the back room and called that a ballot box at table four had jammed, and that it had to be cleared before the noon rush or they would lose an hour of voting, and would Charlie bring the spare seal and the logbook. She went, and Priya and Marcos came with her, and for ten minutes the three of them knelt on the linoleum under the fluorescent lights, coaxing the mechanism loose while the officer recorded each step, and Marcos's grandmother offered, from her folding chair, the observation that in her village they had once counted votes by lamplight because the power had failed, and nobody had thought to complain. The box gave way at last with a click, the seal went on, and the first voters of the noon rush were already filing in.

At eight that evening, when the doors were locked and the counting began, Charlie sat on the stage steps between Priya and Marcos, watching the officers open the boxes under the pool of lamplight as though excavating a stratum of the day, layer after layer of folded paper, each one a private decision now becoming a public number. Priya leaned against the wall with her phone in her lap, waiting for news from home, where the counting had already begun. Marcos had his phone open to the palace photograph again. "I still think ours is better," he said quietly. "I still think ours is," Priya said, and neither of them sounded angry anymore. Charlie said nothing, because she had not decided; she only knew that in three years she would walk through these doors herself, and that she would be thinking, all the way to the booth, about what exactly her one vote was choosing. The officer called out the first total, and all three of them leaned forward to hear it.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, launch angles that add up to 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60 degrees, give the same range on level ground at the same speed.
story:
The projectile launcher sat on the picnic table like something borrowed from a world with more rules than this one. Annabelle had carried it from Mr. Okafor's room after last bell, along with a bag of yellow practice balls and a data sheet she was supposed to fill in for Monday. Marcus had come because he said he had nothing else to do, which was true for both of them, and because the playground behind the elementary school had the longest stretch of flat ground either of them knew of, the rubber safety surface running unbroken from the swings to the fence.

She set the first launch at thirty degrees, cranked the spring to the same notch she would use all afternoon, and fired. The ball rose in a low, efficient arc and struck the ground four tiles from the table, bouncing once against the edge of a hopscotch court. Marcus wrote the distance on his hand because the data sheet had blown under the seesaw. Then, before she could reset the angle, he turned the dial himself, all the way up to sixty degrees, and stepped back with his arms crossed.

"You're going to launch it straight up and waste the whole trial," she said.

"It'll go farther. It's higher. More height, more distance." He said it the way he said most things, as though the assertion were the evidence.

She let him have it, partly because she was tired of arguing with him and partly because a small, ungenerous part of her wanted to watch the ball drop short so she could be right in peace. He fired. The ball climbed, a lazy, towering path that seemed to promise everything, hung for a moment at the top, and then came down and struck the ground at almost exactly the same tile. Marcus walked over and stood on the spot. He walked back and stood where the first ball had landed. He put a pebble on each mark and looked at her.

"Same place," he said. "That's broken. The launcher's broken."

Annabelle crouched at the two pebbles and measured the gap between them with her hand, which came to about the width of her palm, close enough that a windy day or a careless read could account for it. In her notebook she had been separating each launch into horizontal and vertical components, the method Mr. Okafor had drilled until it felt less like math and more like a filing system, a taxonomy of motion where sideways and up-down lived in separate drawers and never touched. She had trusted the drawers without ever wondering what they meant together. Now she looked at the two pebbles and felt the drawers sliding open at once.

"Thirty and sixty," she said slowly. "They add up to ninety." She said it again to hear it outside her head, then fired the launcher herself at forty-five to have a third mark, which landed past both pebbles, and she stood over the three points in the fading light not saying anything, because she did not yet want to predicate an answer on two measurements and a hunch. Marcus asked her what ninety had to do with anything, and she said she didn't know yet, exactly, only that the numbers were not a coincidence, and he pulled his sweatshirt around himself and waited, which for Marcus was a kind of apology.

While she fired the two angles a second and third time to see if the pebbles kept agreeing, she found herself thinking about last spring, when she had dropped the idea of tutoring at the writing center in order to take a second science elective.
